items.title: IGR predicts drawdowns will be major source of retirement income
items.teaser: The report states that drawing down accumulated superannuation will become an increasingly significant part of retirement income for many retirees and is estimated to increase from 2.5 per cent of GDP in 2025–26 to 5.8 per cent of GDP in 2065–66.
items.brief_text: The report states that drawing down accumulated superannuation will become an increasingly significant part of retirement income for many retirees and is estimated to increase from 2.5 per cent of GDP in 2025–26 to 5.8 per cent of GDP in 2065–66. The proportion of people with accounts in the retirement phase, from which they are drawing a superannuation pension, will increase 13.9 percentage points (from 11.6 per cent in 2025–26 to 25.5 per cent in 2065–66). By comparison, the proportion of the population over 65 will increase by only seven percentage points (from 17.8 per cent to 24.8 per cent). “The purpose of the superannuation system is to ensure a dignified retirement. A continued policy focus that encourages accumulated superannuation savings to be drawn on effectively during retirement will help to fulfill the goal of supplementing the Age Pension as a source of retirement income and drive higher living standards in retirement,” the report stated. “The superannuation system will support a higher standard of living in retirement and reduce reliance on the Age Pension. Growing balances will result in superannuation becoming the primary source of retirement income for many retirees.” The report also noted that many recent retirees retain substantial superannuation balances at the end of their lives for multiple reasons, including complexities of navigating the superannuation system, the fear of exhausting savings and the “nest egg” framing of superannuation. The median superannuation balance for people aged 65 and over in the year before death in 2022–23 was $76,000, with around a quarter of balances exceeding $250,000. “The Government is progressing reforms to support retirees make better use of their superannuation savings and strengthen the role of superannuation as a source of retirement income as the system matures,” it said. “Over time, this is expected to improve living standards in retirement. By encouraging retirees to draw on their superannuation savings in retirement, the reforms help ensure that the benefits earned during working lives, and the tax concessions that support them, flow to the targeted generation.” The IGR also revealed that balances at retirement will continue increasing as the system matures. Between 2014 and 2024, the median superannuation balance for individuals aged 65–69 rose 77 per cent, from $115,000 to $204,000 in nominal terms. By the end of the medium term, this is projected to approach $450,000. This reflects returns on superannuation balances and a growing number of individuals who can retire having benefited from compulsory superannuation over a significant portion of their working lives (Chart 6.7). Furthermore, superannuation tax concessions as a proportion of GDP are projected to increase from around 1.7 per cent in 2025–26 to 2.7 per cent in 2065–66, driven by earnings tax concessions. The value of revenue forgone from superannuation tax concessions is projected to overtake expenditure on the Age Pension in the late 2030s. As superannuation assets are assumed to grow faster than GDP growth, earnings concessions are projected to increase as a share of GDP in the long term, rising from around 0.9 per cent of GDP in 2025–26 to 1.7 per cent of GDP in 2065–66. In comparison, contributions concessions (such as employer contributions and voluntary pre-tax contributions) represent a more stable share of GDP. They are driven by the same factors that drive Australia’s GDP, wage growth and the size of the workforce. Financial advice will become more critical, complex David Lane, Head of Wealth Advisory at Focus Partners Australia said the IGR highlights a future where Australians are living longer, retirement is lasting longer, and financial decisions are becoming increasingly complex. “With life expectancy projected to reach 89.5 years for women and 86.1 years for men by 2065–66, and the number of Australians aged 85 and over expected to triple, the importance of proactive financial planning has never been greater,” Lane said. “Qualified financial advisers play a critical role in helping Australians navigate this complexity through integrated advice covering superannuation, investments, tax, retirement income, risk management, estate planning and succession strategies. As longevity increases, the value of holistic financial advice becomes more important than ever.” Lane said the report also highlights the growing divide between the wealth and opportunities of our older and younger generations. “Due in part to the strength of superannuation, and the growth in wealth, the report predicts that the proportion of older Australians receiving an Age Pension or income support payment will fall from 66 per cent currently to 52 per cent by 2066. This will lead to a projected decline in Government spending on the Age and Service Pensions from 2.3 per cent of GDP to 1.8 per cent of GDP by 2066,” he said. “Wealth accumulation is shaped by factors such as home ownership, investment strategies, and superannuation contributions. However, younger generations face new challenges, including slower wealth growth and barriers to entering the property market. As a result, tailored financial advice is essential to help individuals make informed decisions, optimise their savings, and build a secure financial foundation. Many families have become more active in planning for wealth transfer during life, rather than leaving large estates, and this trend is likely to continue to be more prominent.” Blake Briggs, CEO of the Financial Services Council, said the report contains the good news that Australians are living longer and this underlines the importance of a retirement system that works to provide Australians with an adequate and dignified retirement. “The other piece of good news is that Australia’s superannuation system will deliver for Australians in terms of higher balances in retirement and a lower call on Commonwealth aged pension spending as a percentage of GDP.” “However, the report acknowledges that a key driver of intergenerational inequity currently is the fact that young Australians are shut out of the housing market. The report shows home ownership among households aged 25-29 has fallen 17 per cent over the past four decades, with around 250,000 fewer young households owning a home than if 1981 ownership rates had been maintained.” He added the IGR also makes clear that Australia faces significant long term economic challenges, including slower economic and population growth, an ageing population and continued weak productivity growth which will make it harder to sustain rising living standards and meet the growing fiscal costs of an ageing population. “Governments will need to tackle the housing and economic challenges through reforms that support investment, productivity, and economic growth. This is key to maintaining public confidence, including preventing superannuation being identified as the solution to Australia’s economic challenges,” he said. “It is important to recognise, however, that the report demonstrates that Australia’s superannuation system is playing its important role by supporting higher retirement incomes and reducing pressure on future generations.”
items.ai_summary: • **Drawdowns** from superannuation are expected to rise from 2.5% to 5.8% of GDP by 2065–66. • Advisers should prepare clients for retirement income strategies that rely more on superannuation pensions than the Age Pension.

items.title: CPA urges super funds to solve retirement phase or risk locking trillions out of the economy
items.teaser: Richard Webb, CPA Australia Superannuation Lead, said the new Retirement Standard from Association of Super Funds Australia comes amid concerns that many retirees are reluctant to draw on their super savings, despite Australia managing one of the world’s largest retirement asset pools.
items.brief_text: Richard Webb, CPA Australia Superannuation Lead, said the new Retirement Standard from Association of Super Funds Australia comes amid concerns that many retirees are reluctant to draw on their super savings, despite Australia managing one of the world’s largest retirement asset pools. “That’s exactly what the retirement standard measures. It focuses on the income retirees need to fund a comfortable or modest lifestyle, not simply the amount of super they have accumulated,” he said. Webb said Australia’s superannuation system had delivered impressive results and has helped build a retirement savings pool of around $4.5 trillion, but the retirement phase remained a major weakness. “For all the success of Australia’s superannuation system in building one of the world’s largest pools of retirement savings, the industry continues to struggle with the most important transition of all: paying members an income when they retire,” he said. “The uncomfortable reality is that super funds have become very good at collecting contributions and growing balances, but far less effective at helping retirees convert those balances into sustainable income streams that they feel comfortable spending.” Research from ASIC in 2025 highlighted a lack of consistency on how retirees should be supported in retirement, with no agreed best-practice approach to retirement income products, retirement income strategies or large-scale advice delivery. “As a result, many retirees are left to navigate a complex set of choices about account-based pensions, longevity risks and drawdown rates on their own,” Webb said. “The consequences extend beyond retirement and poses broader economic challenges. This is not just a superannuation issue. It’s an economic issue. There’s a risk that trillions of dollars remain locked away in retirement savings simply because the onus is on retirees to switch their retirement income on.” Webb added that if Australians are overwhelmed with paperwork when attempting to draw down their super, the economy misses out on spending, investment and productive growth. “The confidence in the long-term future of the superannuation system should not be taken for granted, particularly among younger Australians,” he said “Public confidence in compulsory super will depend on whether Australians can see the system helping people achieve a better retirement, not simply higher balances during their working lives.” He continued that Australians navigate the shift from accumulating savings to spending them should now be a central priority for policymakers, regulators and super funds. “We’ve spent decades building one of the world’s most successful retirement savings systems. The next challenge is ensuring that entering a secure and dignified retirement is as simple and effective as the process of saving for it,” he said. “Australians should not have to navigate a complex maze of products, rules and decisions just to access an income from the savings they’ve spent a lifetime building. The system must do more to help retirees convert their balances into secure, sustainable retirement income.”
items.ai_summary: • **Australia’s superannuation system manages $4.5 trillion**, but retirees struggle to convert savings into sustainable income. • **Super funds must improve retirement income strategies** to help members spend their savings comfortably and avoid locking trillions out of the economy.

items.title: Pacific AM to land SMA solutions Down Under, appoints investment chief
items.teaser: Pacific Portfolio Solutions, the related body corporate of Pacific Asset Management, will bring the latter's SMA solutions to Australia from the UK, welcoming an industry stalwart to chart the course.
items.brief_text: Pacific Portfolio Solutions (PPS), the related body corporate of Pacific Asset Management (PAM), will bring the latter's separately managed account (SMA) solutions to Australia from the UK, welcoming an industry stalwart to chart the course. Both PPS and PAM are wholly owned subsidiaries of the ASX-listed Pinnacle Investment Management. The initial PPS offering will include the Pinnacle SMA range, comprising Moderate, Balanced, Income, Growth, High Growth, and Listed Growth portfolios, built exclusively from Pinnacle affiliates' actively managed strategies, the firm said. PAM chief executive Matt Lamb said he is looking forward to bringing those capabilities to Australia. "We're bringing something distinctive to Australian managed accounts with PAM's proven multi-asset process and implementation technology," Lamb said. "Being part of the broader Pinnacle group uniquely positions the team to draw on the breadth of expertise across the group's high-quality affiliated fund managers and the strength of its institutional infrastructure." To support the launch, PPS has appointed former Perpetual chief investment officer Kyle Lidbury to lead it Australia-based investment team. Financial Standard reported on the appointment in March , but Pinnacle did not disclose his position at the time. In the newly created role of chief investment officer, Lidbury will oversee PPS' managed account portfolio construction, asset allocation, and adviser investment communications. Lidbury has more than two decades of financial services experience spanning investment research and portfolio management across the industry, including senior leadership roles at Perpetual, NAB Asset Management, MLC and Lendlease. He said he is excited to bring established investment capabilities and technology of PAM to the Australian market tailored for local financial advisers and their clients. "Pacific combines specialist investment expertise with modern technology, enabling us to implement investment decisions and adjust portfolio positioning with a level of efficiency and flexibility I have not previously seen in the Australian market," Lidbury said. Meanwhile, Pinnacle head of managed accounts David Wright said: "Kyle brings deep investment expertise and a strong understanding of the needs of financial advisers." "He combines his portfolio construction and asset allocation experience with an ability to explain investment decisions clearly and communicate what they mean for client portfolios." Lamb added that he is "delighted to have Kyle leading the Australia investment team as we build on our success in the UK market." In the coming months, Lidbury will also help to introduce the Pacific Core range - PAM's flagship UK model portfolio offering - to Australia through managed account solutions.
items.ai_summary: • **Pacific AM will launch SMA solutions in Australia**, including Moderate, Balanced, Income, Growth, High Growth, and Listed Growth portfolios. • **Kyle Lidbury has been appointed as chief investment officer** to lead the investment team and oversee portfolio construction and adviser communications.

items.brief_text: Praemium will bring forward its leadership transition at board level, with its current chair stepping down as the platform and portfolio administration business continues to expand its focus on high-net-worth investors and technology. Matthew Quinn will replace Barry Lewin as chair, with Lewin bringing forward his departure and stepping down from the role effective 22 September 2026. Praemium said Lewin had overseen significant growth during his tenure, with the board thanking him for his contribution, leadership and commitment to the company and its people. Research from Praemium and Core Data published in August found 80% of high-net-worth investors who work with an adviser had already used artificial intelligence (AI) for financial tasks, including financial education, comparing investment strategies and sense-checking advice. However, only 29% said they would manage their portfolio themselves if given access to the same tools as their adviser, while roughly seven in 10 would still prefer to retain their adviser's guidance. The research also found 86% believe the human adviser-client relationship will remain important in an AI enabled future, with most favouring a model that combines human advice with AI support. Australia's high-net-worth market grew 10% to 1.33 million households during the period covered by the research, while total investable wealth increased 8.4% to $4.6 trillion. More than 120,000 households entered the HNW segment, with more than seven in 10 investors using a financial adviser or wealth manager. The chair transition comes as Praemium reported total funds under administration of $77.9 billion for FY26 , up 21.1% from the previous year. Platform FUA rose 10.8% to $34 billion, while non-custodial portfolio administration business Scope+ increased 30.5% to 12,793 in portfolio numbers. The company has identified HNW segment as a key area of focus as it continues to grow its platform and administration business.

items.title: Advisers missing the third retirement risk, warns Aged Care Steps
items.teaser: Aged Care Steps is urging advisers to plan for frailty risk alongside longevity and sequencing risk, after its latest whitepaper found older Australians are spending more of their retirement with severe disability.
items.brief_text: Aged Care Steps is urging advisers to plan for frailty risk alongside longevity and sequencing risk, after its latest whitepaper found older Australians are spending more of their retirement with severe disability. Its Planning for the Third Phase of Retirement report found the expected period of severe disability for a man aged 65 rose from 3.5 years in 2018 to 4.6 years in 2022, or from 17.5 per cent to 22 per cent of retirement. Women saw the period rise from 5.5 to 6.4 years, or from 25 per cent to 28 per cent of retirement. “During the frailty period, the rising incidence of dementia, increasing care costs and greater burden on family are making aged care decisions more complex and consequential, creating both a client need and an advice opportunity,” Aged Care Steps director Assyat David said. Aged Care Steps estimates the frailty years make up 17 to 24 per cent of retirement on average and said income needs are more likely to follow a U-shape than the straight-line retirement plans have typically used. The average refundable accommodation deposit has risen 15 per cent in 18 months to $604,919, according to the paper, while the maximum permissible interest rate for daily accommodation payment has gone from 7.78 per cent to 8.43 per cent in a year. In one case study, a single homeowner with approximately $1.2 million in assets moves into a $605,000 room and pays by daily accommodation payment rather than a lump sum. Her first-year accommodation cost comes to approximately $51,384, which is $6,882 more than a year earlier. “The focus has traditionally been on building a retirement income stream and managing risks like longevity, liquidity, investment risk and sequencing risk, but clients face another risk that receives far less attention, frailty risk,” Aged Care Steps director Louise Biti said. Aged Care Steps’ Burden Conversation checklist tells advisers to revisit the discussion after major health or family changes and at annual reviews, and to check whether their modelling covers care costs in the frailty years. “The burden conversation can help clients clarify their preferences and understand their options before decisions become urgent – giving them greater choice, control and confidence, while reducing the risk of rushed decisions, family conflict and avoidable financial stress,” Biti said. NAB’s Professional Services Performance Era report found 81 per cent of practices offer retirement planning but only 42 per cent provide aged care advice , while 35 per cent of advisers rank aged care among their top growth areas. “Advisers who focus only on investments and early-stage retirement may lose relevance as clients seek comprehensive advice and much-needed reassurance to support their transition through the phases of retirement,” David said.
items.ai_summary: • Severe disability period for men aged 65 rose from 3.5 to 4.6 years **(increase)** • Advisers should consider frailty risk alongside longevity and sequencing risk **(advice focus)**

items.brief_text: AGS Financial Group, a Sydney financial planning and accounting firm, has completed the full acquisition of Hartley Financial. Hartley will bring two NSW and one Melbourne office to AGS Financial Group with the acquisition expected to add around $2.6 million in annual revenue. AGS, which is an authorised representative of Akumin Financial Planning, aims to grow geographically and attract new talents amid a strained supply of financial planners. Synergies and continuity But AGS says the M&A move is not simply about scale, and that Hartley represents a structural and cultural fit. Both businesses deal with financial planning, taxation, accounting, mortgages and lending. A company statement also states the two firms favour long-term relationships rather than individual transactions. “What attracted us to Hartley was that we didn’t need to change how they work to make this fit,” said Paul Bolstad, CEO of AGS Financial Group. “They run the same integrated model we do, with planning, tax, accounting and lending under one roof, and they hold the same values. Their focus has never been the single transaction, it’s the end outcome and the relationship behind it.” Continuity is hailed as a keyword, with adviser, broker and accountant relationships expected to remain unchanged, along with existing phone numbers, offices, files and engagements. “Clients on both sides should see continuity rather than disruption,” affirmed Bolstad. Meanwhile, David Hartley, founder of the eponymous company, is set to stay involved through the transition although what happens after both businesses are fully integrated remains open-ended. And, in the M&A process, Hartley’s Mascot office in NSW was closed with clients able to access the firm in nearby offices in Picton, Sutherland and Parkdale or online. AGS also has its own offices in North Sydney, Norwest, Hurstville, Miranda, South Melbourne and Brisbane. M&A rationale in a saturated market According to an AGS statement, the acquisition means more access for Hartley when it comes to retirement planning, wills, estate planning, aged care advice, risk and insurance. “Clients want advisers who are reachable and who understand their community, but they also want the depth of a group that can handle the tax return, the mortgage and the retirement plan” said Bolstad. For AGS, one of the main rationales behind the M&A move is geographical expansion. Speaking with Money Management, Alex Berlee, co-founder and director at AGS Group, said his firm was looking for new footprints in areas where it already had prospects. “The main thing we gained is the geographical presence, we had contacts but not necessarily a local presence,” said Berlee. Another significant incentive was the need for qualified financial professionals in a strained market. “There’s less financial planners than there used to be, but the client demand hasn’t disappeared,” added Berlee, pointing to the impact of the Royal Commission. The Royal Commission into Misconduct in the Banking, Superannuation and Financial Services Industry led to major changes to the financial advice profession. One of them was tougher education and professional standards for financial advisers. AGS states that it does grow financial advisers internally, but that it wanted to go further with the Hartley acquisition. “When we can find a business that has existing people, existing clients, and that we can help be more efficient; that’s a good way for us to grow our advising team,” Berlee concluded.

items.title: Pinnacle affiliate appoints former Perpetual CIO
items.teaser: Former Perpetual chief investment officer, Kyle Lidbury, has departed to take on a new role at Pinnacle affiliate Pacific Portfolio Solutions (PPS).
items.brief_text: Former Perpetual chief investment officer, Kyle Lidbury, has departed to take on a new role at Pinnacle affiliate Pacific Portfolio Solutions (PPS). At PPS, he now holds the same position and leads the Australia-based investment team, overseeing managed account portfolio construction, asset allocation, and adviser relations. PPS is the related body corporate of London-based Pacific Asset Management (PAM). Both are wholly owned by Pinnacle Investment Management Group which took a 100 per cent stake back in February 2026, after initially taking a 21 per cent stake in 2024. Lidbury spent 14 years at Perpetual in a variety of roles including CIO, head of investment research and general manager of research and operations and previously spent three years at NAB and four years at MLC. He had been on gardening leave at Perpetual over the past few months. With Lidbury’s appointment, PPS is set to develop a variety of separately managed accounts (SMA), including moderate, balanced, income, growth, high growth and listed growth portfolios for advisers. Matt Lamb, CEO of UK-based PAM, said this brings a new offering for Aussie advisers. “We’re bringing something distinctive to Australian managed accounts with PAM’s proven multi-asset process and implementation technology. We’re delighted to have [Lidbury] leading the Australia investment team as we build on our success in the UK market.” He also stressed the importance of maintaining strong relationships with advisers, as part of the role. “[Lidbury] combines his portfolio construction and asset allocation experience with an ability to explain investment decisions clearly and communicate what they mean for client portfolios,” continued Lamb. Looking ahead, PPS will also bring PAM’s ‘Pacific Core Range’ to Australia. The Pacific Core Growth Range consists of five highly diversified multi-asset class portfolios which will be tailored for the local wealth market Earlier in August , PAM had said it was looking to the advisory market to expand its model portfolio business and bring its UK learnings to Australia. This is now complete with PPS set to offer SMA solutions for local financial advisers and their clients, under the Pinnacle umbrella. “[PPS can] draw on the breadth of expertise across the group’s high-quality affiliated fund managers and the strength of its institutional infrastructure.” affirmed Lamb. Currently, PAM runs an integrated investment team across its Sydney and London office. “It’s exciting to be working with the teams across the UK and here in Australia. Pacific combines specialist investment expertise with modern technology, enabling us to implement investment decisions and adjust portfolio positioning with a level of efficiency and flexibility I have not previously seen in the Australian market,” Lidbury added. Perpetual has appointed David Blunt to the CIO role in an acting capacity.

items.title: Retirement confidence lags as investors turn to AI
items.teaser: Retirement has emerged as a central for investors globally, but a lack of confidence and financial literacy is keeping many savers on the sidelines, according to Amundi's latest global investor study.
items.brief_text: Retirement has emerged as a central concern for investors globally, but a lack of confidence and financial literacy is keeping many savers on the sidelines, according to Amundi's latest global investor study. The third edition of Amundi's Decoding Investors study surveyed 17,000 respondents across 26 countries and found personal savings and investments are expected to provide 42% of investor's retirement income, ahead of state provisions and workplace pensions. However, only 23% of investors said they were very confident about achieving long-term financial security, down from 26% a year earlier. Professional advice is a significant factor in retirement confidence, with half of advised investors saying they were very confident about funding retirement, compared with 14% of those who have never accessed advice. Amundi found 43% of savers expected to start investing within the next 12 months, rising to 62% among those aged 21 to 30. However, 39% said fear of losing money remained a barrier, contributing to continued high cash holdings. The study also highlighted a gap between perceived and actual investment knowledge, with 70% of investors who described themselves as experts failing to correctly answer three basic financial literacy questions. Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly becoming part of investors decision making, with 70% saying they had used AI to help make investment decisions. Of those, 59% had acted on AI recommendations. Regular use of AI assistance for investment ideas or information also quadrupled over the past year to 19%, while 46% of investors said they sought investment information through influencers. Amundi deputy general manager and head of clients group Fannie Wurtz said the findings highlighted the challenge of helping more savers participate in capital markets. "While funding retirement becomes a central concern for households globally, the third edition of our Decoding Investors study highlights a pressing challenge: helping more savers become investors and enter capital markets," Wurtz said. "For our industry, this means strengthening trust, improving access to investor education notably through digital channels and offering simple, transparent and accessible solutions." More than 60% of investors said they had access to at least some professional financial advice, with 59% receiving all or part of their advice online. Wurtz said other contributing factors included demographic changes, growing pressures and changes in savings landscape. "As demographic change, growing pressure on retirement systems and digitalisation reshape the savings landscape, individuals are increasingly being called upon to take greater responsibility for their long-term financial security," Wurtz said. "The challenge - and the opportunity - is to help more savers become investors, putting their savings to work for the future. Many people understand the importance of investing, yet too many still hesitate to take action."
items.ai_summary: • **23%** of investors are very confident about retirement, down from 26% last year; • Advisers can boost confidence by providing professional advice, as **half of advised investors** are very confident

items.brief_text: UBS is renaming its not-for-profit segment to a ‘for purpose’ division as Anthony Hamawi is appointed from JBWere to head up the department. Although not-for-profit missions will be a part of the broader ‘for purpose’ segment, UBS adapted its name by bringing forward a broader ‘purpose’ concept. According to its website , the bank’s purpose is twofold. “Reimagining the power of investing” and “Connecting people for a better world.” UBS said it aims to connect people and ideas to be more efficient and innovative. items.title: Vietnam joins FTSE Russell emerging market index
items.teaser: Vietnam has officially joined the FTSE Russell Global Equity Index Series, marking a new phase for its capital market as it moves from frontier to Secondary Emerging Market status.
items.brief_text: Vietnam has officially joined the FTSE Russell Global Equity Index Series, marking a new phase for its capital market as it moves from frontier to Secondary Emerging Market status. The reclassification took effect on 21 September 2026, following years of reforms to Vietnam's market infrastructure, regulatory framework and access for international investors. The milestone was marked at a conference in Hanoi attended by 200 delegates, including representatives from global investment firms, custodians, securities companies and other market participants. Vietnam Finance Minister Ngo Van Tuan said the reclassification would broaden access to international capital while raising expectations around market quality and regulatory capacity. "Vietnam is ready to listen to international organisations and pursue further bold reforms to build a transparent, safe, and efficient capital market that remains sustainably attractive," Tuan said. The government intends to continue capital market development through 2030, with a longer-term vision to 2045, including measures to improve liquidity, modernise infrastructure, strengthen risk management and diversify investment products. UK ambassador to Vietnam Iain Grant Frew said the reclassification reflected the country's economic transformation and efforts to build a deeper and more internationally connected capital market. The World Bank also welcomed the reforms, with Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos country director Mariam Sherman describing the reclassification as a "milestone, not the final goal." Sherman said deeper capital markets could attract private and institutional capital, diversifying financing beyond the banking system and direct long-term saving towards productive investment. FTSE Russell said more than US$22 trillion in assets use its indices as benchmarks. The index provider and London Stock Exchange Group will continue working with Vietnam as it develops its capital market, with a focus on supporting international capital flows and a deeper and more resilient market.

items.title: How Nvidia’s Jensen Huang could reshape geopolitics for investors
items.teaser: Stanford University professor Stephen Kotkin says computing power will become the key geopolitical contest between the US and China, predicting Nvidia founder and chief executive Jensen Huang will become an increasingly central figure in international relations.
items.brief_text: Computing power, not broad economic sanctions, is the one lever historian Stephen Kotkin argues the US can pull that might actually work against China. In a keynote address to the Top1000funds.com Fiduciary Investors Symposium at Stanford University, Kotkin suggested Nvidia’s Jensen Huang could be the one figure whose next move reshapes that balance. Kotkin, who is the Kleinheinz Senior Fellow at Stanford’s Hoover Institution, said the US position in computing power is the exception to his general scepticism about sanctions. “We’ve got about 75 per cent going to 80 per cent of computing power in the United States,” he said. “I would be seduced into thinking that’s a big trend line where money is going to be made, not just tomorrow, but maybe after tomorrow.” That dominance matters, he added, “for as long as computing power is the limiting factor in AI”, though he was careful to note he does not know how long that will remain true. But “there are many places” where broad economic sanctions could backfire, or only have “a temporary impact, if any, with perverse and unintended consequences,” he said. “It reduces trust in the dollar.” Prior to his address to the symposium, Kotkin met with Conexus Financial founder Colin Tate AM and chair Geoff Lloyd in his Hoover Tower office on campus at Stanford and expanded on the implications of the geopolitical landscape for investors. Shifting ground In his symposium address, Kotkin cautioned that the compute advantage is not static. He pointed to a string of looming shifts in chip packaging, memory and energy – South Korean packaging and memory, Taiwanese packaging, and fusion power, which he said “looks impossible now because of tritium, but that’s coming” – any one of which could alter who controls the underlying infrastructure. Battery chemistry was another example: “Lithium batteries disappear, sodium batteries displace them. So, it’s just salt,” he said, describing how quickly a seemingly indispensable material can be supplanted. He argued that the US advantage is to replicate, citing France’s difficulty finding sites for AI data centres. France’s search turned up only ten possible locations nationwide, he said, five of them under military control, which is a supply constraint he described simply as “insane.” Kotkin singled out Nvidia’s chief executive as pivotal to how the contest develops. “We have Nvidia and Jensen Huang,” he said. “Jensen’s in some ways the central actor of this whole story, especially if he does open weights [AI], which we suspect is his next move, to try to take over the entire global ecosystem against his customers who are buying the chips.” Even as he named computing power as the trend line worth backing, Kotkin warned against treating any trend line as fixed. He recalled the consensus barely two decades ago that Chinese economic growth would compound at eight to ten per cent a year “kind of forever” until it overtook the US. “Those trend lines look stupid right now,” he said. “There’s so much that happens in material science that upsets the trend lines.” Disclaimer: This article was composed with the assistance of generative AI, but edited, approved and fact-checked by the Conexus Financial editorial team.

items.title: Privacy reforms well-meaning but mustn’t increase advice complexity: FAAA
items.teaser: Responding to the Government’s consultation of the Privacy Amendment (Personal Data Protection) Bill 2026, the FAAA has argued that further refinement is needed as the current proposal could add further data consent requirements for advisers without delivering any tangible consumer benefit.
items.brief_text: Responding to the Government’s consultation of the Privacy Amendment (Personal Data Protection) Bill 2026 , the FAAA has argued that further refinement is needed as the current proposal could add further data consent requirements for advisers without delivering any tangible consumer benefit. The nature of financial advice relationships means they collect and store sensitive information about clients to be used later as advisers will rely on both previously collected and new information to facilitate service. Pointing to this in the submission, the FAAA argued that the legislation needs to make clear that the “collection, use, disclosure and retention of personal information” is reasonably necessary in order for advisers to meet their existing statutory, regulatory, professional and dispute resolution obligations. “Financial advisers are already subject to extensive statutory and professional obligations that require them to collect, verify, retain and use personal information throughout the adviser-client relationship.” “An overly narrow interpretation of the data minimisation requirement could discourage appropriate fact-finding and create uncertainty about the information advisers can reasonably collect to satisfy their obligations under the Best Interests Duty and the Financial Planners and Advisers Code of Ethics, both of which require advisers to obtain and consider sufficient information about the client before providing advice.” As such, it recommended that the proposed legislation be amended to reflect this need as the collection of ‘fair and reasonable’ data. It also warned that stipulations about requiring voluntary, informed, current, specific and unambiguous consent from clients could create uncertainty for advisers because they are often operating within an ongoing client arrangement. The consequence could introduce the obligation, perceived or otherwise, for advisers to obtain fresh consent any time personal information is used for a review, implementation activity or related advice purposes. “We are concerned that this obligation reflects a transactional relationship rather than an ongoing professional relationship, creating additional compliance costs and client friction without necessarily improving privacy outcomes. “The framework should recognise that, where a client enters into an ongoing advice relationship, consent can be obtained at the commencement of the engagement for reasonably foreseeable advice, implementation and review activities. “Renewed specific consent should only be required where there is a material change in purpose, scope or parties involved.” There are also concerns it could infringe on referral arrangements because the Bill introduces a new requirement for consent before an organisation ‘trades’ personal information, with a ‘trade’ encapsulating disclosures for money or other consideration, or for the purposes of direct marketing, as explained by the FAAA. “Holistic financial advice frequently involves an adviser referring client information to another specialist financial adviser such as a risk adviser for life insurance advice, a mortgage broker for a home loan, an accountant for tax advice, or an aged care specialist for placement advice, referrals that are made because the client has asked the adviser to help arrange these services. “We would not describe this as a trade; however, we are concerned about what might be captured under this term.” Among the concerns and recommendations, the association said that, while it understands the objectives of modernising Australia’s privacy laws as a means of strengthening consumer trust and protection, it suggested that the proposed measures would add further complexity to an already highly-regulated profession, compounding the existing administrative burden and creating unnecessary uncertainty. “Financial advisers are entrusted with some of the most sensitive information Australians hold, and a modern, workable privacy framework is squarely in the interests of the advice profession and its clients. “However, the FAAA considers that the reforms, as currently drafted, would benefit from further clarification of how the new principles-based standards are intended to interact with the extensive, preexisting regulatory obligations that already govern the collection, use, disclosure and retention of client information in fields such as financial advice. “Without this clarity, there is a real risk of unnecessary regulatory duplication and uncertainty, without a commensurate improvement in privacy outcomes for clients.”

items.title: The New Class of Adviser: Vertical integration and the case for advice practices
items.teaser: On 19 August, Financial Services Minister Dr Daniel Mulino announced, among other reforms, that the government would push ahead the ‘New Class of Adviser’ (NCA), but they would be limited to superannuation funds and insurance providers.
items.brief_text: On 19 August, Financial Services Minister Dr Daniel Mulino announced, among other reforms, that the government would push ahead the ‘New Class of Adviser’ (NCA), but they would be limited to superannuation funds and insurance providers. The FAAA has long argued that, should NCAs be introduced, that advice practices should be allowed to employ them in order to support the industry in delivering scoped or simple advice. Phil Anderson, FAAA general manager of policy, advocacy and standards, said the association was “disappointed with the outcome”, but said that there was still hope that advice practices may be rolled into the program in three years, when the minister has committed to a review of the stipulation. There isn’t a solid explanation at this point as to why they were left out, however FAAA chief executive Sarah Abood suggested it may be down to an abundance of caution while the government understands how NCAs will operate in practice. “I think the minister is aware or has a view that this is a very new thing, and his instinct was to kind of start small and then maybe grow it over time. But he wasn’t explicit in the speech about the thinking behind it, so I’m meta-analysing what he said,” Abood told an FAAA roundtable attended by ifa. Anderson added: “I think there’s there was a focus on the risk of downside and the perception that that needed to be tightly controlled.” A common thread in discussion since the idea of NCAs were introduced back in the Quality of Advice Review (QAR) has been vertical integration, with some believing it would be a step back to the days when institutions dominated the advice space. However, Abood said the FAAA isn’t against institutions employing NCAs, but they shouldn’t be the only ones who can. “Institutions can offer advice. There’s no law against it. They can choose to take out an AFSL that lets them give financial product advice to consumers, but they see the same challenges we do in terms of the high cost of offering that form of advice, the challenge in hiring enough people to do it,” she said. “There can be a level of vertical integration. There’s no law that says institutions can’t do it now, they can. But they find it expensive and difficult, and a new class would help them, but it would also help us.” Abood added: “We don’t object to institutions being able to do more for their clients, but we don’t think they should be the only organisations that are able to do it.” How would NCAs benefit advisers? Abood believes that if advice practices were able to employ NCAs, the role could serve as a lead-in to becoming a fully qualified financial adviser and help foster the next generation of the profession, creating a kind of “training ground” that is currently sorely lacking. At the same time, it would give practices the ability to service a broader range of needs, be a tool to engage with clients’ children, proving a greater value proposition, and make advice more accessible which is the goal at the heart of the NCA proposition. “The framing of the new class was about making advice more accessible and affordable to that point before, but advice is broader than just what investment option can I pick in my super fund,” Abood said. “For an advice firm, it’s an opportunity to connect with the children, the grandchildren of your clients, to provide advice in an area where the costs are currently too high to make it possible to do that, and there are lots of advice firms that that I think would appreciate the opportunity to do that. “The other point we would make is that that form of advice would not be vertically integrated, so at the moment the new class of advice, as proposed, would only be offered by vertically integrated institutions. “We think it makes sense to have a form of that advice available to consumers that isn’t solely dependent on the product. We see it as broader than just advice on a particular product, and that’s what our vision would be. And we’re still hopeful that that will get there.” Anderson said NCAs could be used for simple matters and getting the scope right is important, particularly while the education standards remain unclear. “I don’t think we would ever view this as necessarily an opportunity for us to unleash this New Class of Adviser on the Australian population, but as a means of servicing existing clients more efficiently, for where they have relatively simple means,” he said. “We’ve always argued that if this is going to be rolled out, it should be limited to simple advice, which is appropriate given that the education standards will be lower. We’ve always said that retirement advice is not simple advice. “These are some of the challenges that still need to be resolved, but from the start of this, some of our members and some of the practices have said, ‘Well, we do see merit in financial advice practices being able to use the New Class of Adviser’.” One of the more contentious issues surrounding NCAs, though admittedly not the most important, has been the name itself, particularly the use of the word ‘adviser’ in the title. Since the idea was born, they have been called Qualified Advisers, the New Class of Advisers, the New Class of Providers, and a variety of other iterations. Most important, though, is maintaining the protection of the word ‘adviser’ which is currently a legally protected title. “In addition to that, it’s the scope of advice that they can provide, the education standard that applies, and exactly how clients will pay for the services that they provide, if that’s the case at all.” He added: “There’s a lot more detail that needs to be worked out.” There is still no clarity as to why advice practices were excluded from hiring NCAs at this time, but a review is slated for three years after the reforms come into effect. Have you say! ifa is currently running a poll asking Would you employ someone under the proposed ‘New Class of Adviser’ model in your advice practice if you could?

items.title: FAAA flags gaps in discretionary trusts tax reforms, deficient framework
items.teaser: Under the proposed minimum tax on discretionary trust reforms, the Financial Advice Association Australia (FAAA) highlighted concerns over trustees potentially being forced to make "major and largely irreversible decisions" before the rules and guidance have been finalised.
items.brief_text: Under the proposed minimum tax on discretionary trust reforms, the Financial Advice Association Australia (FAAA) highlighted concerns over trustees potentially being forced to make "major and largely irreversible decisions" before the rules and guidance have been finalised. Treasury released the draft legislation on the 30% minimum tax on discretionary trusts in early September, consulting on how the minimum tax will work, what types of trusts and income should be excluded and how a fixed trust should be defined. One of the proposed changes is introducing a new option for discretionary trusts to be exempt from the minimum tax if they elect to make fixed distributions to pre-nominated beneficiaries, as an alternative to roll-over relief. The election would not require a restructure and is not expected to result in state and territory stamp duties. Trustees will also be able to nominate individuals and entities that are capable of benefiting under the trust from 1 July 2028, including eligible companies and trusts, with no limit on the number of beneficiaries that can be nominated. The association believes some of the new pathways proposed are too rigid and could unfairly penalise people who make genuine mistakes or experience normal life events such as family changes, succession planning or circumstances beyond their control. "Important practical issues remain unresolved, including state and territory stamp duty consequences, the treatment of beneficiaries under the excluded election trust (EET) regime, the operation of the roll-over provisions, and the potentially substantial compliance and professional advice costs associated with understanding, implementing and maintaining the new arrangements," the FAAA wrote in its submission. "The FAAA supports appropriately targeted integrity measures but considers that further refinement of the package is necessary before the legislation is enacted." The submission highlighted three pathways trustees of discretionary trusts will need to assess: remaining within the minimum tax regime, choosing the EET model or restructuring under the transitional roll-over option. Treasury stated in the explanatory memorandum it has yet to release further legislation to address residency, CGT, international taxation, administrative and reporting requirements, and integrity considerations. Consequently, the FAAA pointed out taxpayers and their advisers are being asked to evaluate the costs, benefits and risks of each pathway without a complete understanding of how the broader framework will operate in practice. "This is likely to increase complexity, require additional professional advice, and result in significant unnecessary implementation and compliance costs. This uncertainty is particularly significant, given that discretionary trusts are commonly used for a range of non-tax purposes," the association said. It is therefore recommending Treasury to complete the minimum tax framework before commencement and defer key implementation deadlines until taxpayers, and their advisers have sufficient certainty about how the regime will operate. "This would reduce unnecessary complexity and compliance and advice costs, while helping taxpayers make informed decisions about whether restructuring, electing into the EET regime or remaining within the minimum tax framework is appropriate," the FAAA said.
items.ai_summary: • **FAAA highlights gaps in discretionary trusts tax reforms** with concerns over trustees making irreversible decisions before final rules are set; • **Advisers must stay informed on the proposed 30% minimum tax** and consider the new exemption options for discretionary trusts

items.title: What the 2026 Intergenerational Report means for advisers
items.teaser: Focus Partners Australia says this week’s Intergenerational Report highlights a world where Aussies will be living longer and retirement last longer.
items.brief_text: Focus Partners Australia says this week’s Intergenerational Report highlights a world where Aussies will be living longer and retirement last longer. According to the government’s 2026 Intergenerational Report, life expectancy in Australia is projected to reach almost 90 years for women and just over 86.1 years for men by 2066. Released on 21 September, the report projects the outlook for the Australian economy and the Government’s budget to 2065–66. These projections help inform and improve public policy settings to better position Australia for the next 40 years. Meanwhile, the number of Australians aged 85 and over is expected to triple, with consequences for retirement planning amid increased healthcare and aged care considerations. Focus also pointed to more complex wealth transfer decisions if retirement lasts longer. This means that proactive financial planning is even more important, according to Focus Partners Australia. For now, the advice firm says the superannuation system has been effective in building wealth during the accumulation phase of older Aussies. In fact, the report predicts that the proportion of older Australians receiving an Age Pension or income support payment will fall from 66 per cent currently to 52 per cent in 40 years. “This shift means that superannuation will increasingly become the primary source of retirement income, reducing reliance on the Age Pension and placing more responsibility on individuals to manage their financial wellbeing,” commented David Lane, head of wealth advisory at Focus Partners. This creates challenges for the next generations who will also face slower wealth growth and less access to the property market. “Intergenerational equity is being strained by the long-term decline in home ownership,” read the report, pointing out that the absence of home ownership can limit accessible wealth at retirement. The case for advisers Focus Partners argues these elements only reinforce the need for financial advisers. The wealth manager highlights increased complexity across superannuation, investments, tax, retirement income, risk management, estate planning and succession strategies. Combined with a longer timeframe, this would reinforce the need for future retirees to establish a broad strategy for their finances. “As longevity increases, the value of holistic financial advice becomes more important than ever,” said Lane. In his view, professional financial advice helps balance different goals. Namely, income needs, lifestyle goals or the future costs of care. It also supports super holders when facing complex questions around timing, transmission and tax. The government report notably highlighted that future tax changes can be considered as the tax base of working Aussie narrows. Further, larger wealth transfers can require greater preparation. “Many families have become more active in planning for wealth transfer during life, rather than leaving large estates, and this trend is likely to continue to be more prominent” “Estate planning and intergenerational wealth transfer strategies are becoming increasingly important to ensure assets are distributed according to wishes, tax implications are managed, and family members are supported,” continued Lane. Overall, Focus Partners recommends planning financial goals earlier rather than later so individuals can reap the benefit of compounding, and review and adapt their goals before the end of their working years. “Holistic financial advice extends well beyond investment selection. It integrates retirement planning, superannuation, tax optimisation, risk management, estate planning, cash flow management and family wealth strategies,” concluded Focus Partners.
items.ai_summary: • **Life expectancy in Australia is projected to reach 90 years for women and 86.1 years for men by 2066**; • **Retirement planning must adapt to longer lifespans** with increased healthcare and wealth transfer complexities

items.title: Esencia Wealth ads MDA licence through Generation Wealth merger
items.teaser: Esencia Wealth has added a managed discretionary account capability to its arsenal through a merger with Generation Wealth Partners, as it pushes ahead with its growth-by-merger strategy.
items.brief_text: Esencia launched in 2024 following the merger of Advise Wise, Insight Private Wealth, Sovereign Wealth Partners and Randle Advisory, and the addition now of Generation Wealth and its managed discretionary account licence will allow Esencia to broaden its investment capability. Generation principals Peter Lee and Joe Jutrisa join Esencia Wealth as shareholders, partners and senior financial advisers. “The intention for us, at least the medium term, is to continue to operate that [MDA licence], in which most of Peter and Joe’s clients sit, and it provides a potential solution for a cohort of our clients as well,” Esencia Wealth CEO and managing director Matthew Fenning tells Professional Planner . “But our model is not a licensee model; it’s a one integrated firm model. The intention as an advice firm is to continue to run a single licensee model.” Fenning says the plan is to keep both licences for the medium term as it is best for the clients and the simplest way to continue to operate without disruption. “But we’ll spend plenty of time thinking about how we operate that over the long term. But the path of least resistance is it it’s working well. It’s working well for clients. It’s working well for the business. So, we’ll retain that as is for the immediate future.” A benefit of the merger for Generation Wealth is that Esencia absorbs aspects of the day-to-day operation of the business freeing up time that Lee and Jutrisa can dedicate to clients. “There are things that we can invest in that smaller businesses can’t. So, there’s a lot more specialisation available to Peter and Joe and others that helps them in the background to service clients in the foreground,” Fenning says. “There’s a lot of talk about advisor productivity in the market, and that tends to be directed at more clients, and that’s a valid point. But I think what’s not talked about as much is more time and a more personalised opportunity to take more personalised approach with clients.” In a media release Lee said Generation Wealth Partners started under the belief that there was a better way to serve clients and their families “with genuine relationships, personalised advice and a real focus on the long term”. “Joining Esencia Wealth means we can keep delivering on that promise, while giving our clients access to the depth of expertise and resources that come with a growing national firm,” Lee said. Fenning says that his personal experience going from running a small business up until a few years ago to leading Esencia is that it was harder to invest in people and create long term pathways for people to learn, grow and stay with the business. “Having more scale, I suppose, but effectively more money to spend means that you can invest more in people and create more types of opportunities for people, not just linear ones, where I go from client service to associate advisor to advisor, and so on. “But we can create a lot of opportunities for people to work on projects and initiatives for things that they’re interested in. We can create similar opportunities that larger businesses can for people to move around.” Growth strategy and the operating model Esencia has 26 authorised representatives, including the Generation Wealth partners. When it launched in 2024 it had 11. The business has grown from 1000 to 2800 clients since 2024, with 250 coming from the Generation Wealth merger. With a vision to support 10,000 clients nationally, Esencia continues to look for partners with similar values and focus. Esencia has the ambition to be a national business and is currently present in Sydney and recently expanded to Brisbane and Shell Harbour in March and May respectively. The clients that Generation Wealth brings are the sort that the business has supported and advised for a long time. When it comes to mergers, Esencia looks for firms with the same values and vision, “because one mistake, doesn’t matter how many people you have, can be a big distraction for a long time”. Fenning agrees that there is no single operating model what will succeed in the future of financial advice but for Esencia the focus will remain the same: being a strategic financial advice business. “But there’s a place for the larger licensees, and they’ve done a great job of flipping or evolving their model over the course of time,” Fenning says. “All of those different things are going to work as long as the organisations are capable of executing on it and doing a great job that results in good outcomes for clients. “There’s a lot, a lot more opportunity in in financial advice than I think there’s ever been, and that’s good news for everyone.”

items.title: Beyond traditional bucketing: Why advisers are rethinking SMSF retirement strategies
items.teaser: Retirement bucketing strategies have long been a cornerstone of SMSF retirement planning, helping retirees manage sequencing risk by separating short-term spending needs from longer-term growth assets.
items.brief_text: Retirement bucketing strategies have long been a cornerstone of SMSF retirement planning, helping retirees manage sequencing risk by separating short-term spending needs from longer-term growth assets. But new actuarial research suggests advisers may be overlooking an important piece of the retirement income puzzle: guaranteed lifetime income. At a recent webinar hosted by Money Management with Allianz Retire+ , advisers heard how combining traditional bucketing strategies with lifetime income solutions could materially improve retirement outcomes for SMSF members. Independent modelling conducted by Accurium tested more than 3,000 retirement strategy scenarios and found consistent improvements in both retirement income confidence and projected estate values when lifetime income was incorporated into a retirement framework. According to Melanie Dunn, head of actuarial services at Accurium, the findings challenge some of the conventional assumptions underpinning retirement portfolio construction. “The objective of the research was to assess whether retirement bucketing strategies incorporating a lifetime income solution could improve retirement outcomes for SMSF members when compared with more traditional retirement approaches,” she said. The research comes at a time when advisers are being asked to solve increasingly complex retirement challenges. Longer life expectancies, elevated market volatility and uncertainty around future investment returns are forcing many retirees to balance competing objectives: generating sufficient income today while preserving capital for an unknown future. For many SMSF clients, this challenge is magnified by their preference for maintaining control over their investments. SMSF members also tend to have longer investment horizons, significant accumulated assets and a strong desire to retain flexibility, making the retirement income challenge particularly acute. According to Catherine van der Veen, chief distribution and marketing officer at Allianz Retire+, retirement planning is increasingly becoming an income challenge rather than simply an investment challenge. “For years we’ve focused heavily on portfolio construction and investment returns. But the conversations advisers are having with clients today are different,” she said. “Clients want answers to three simple questions: do I have enough, what can I spend, and what will be left for my family? Those questions require a retirement income strategy, not just an investment strategy.” Traditionally, bucketing strategies have sought to manage sequencing risk by creating separate pools of retirement savings. Cash reserves are used to cover immediate spending needs, while defensive and growth assets remain invested over longer periods. The approach has become particularly popular among SMSF investors seeking to avoid selling growth assets during periods of market stress. However, while bucketing can provide valuable protection against sequencing risk, it does not remove longevity risk or guarantee that income will continue throughout retirement. That formed the basis of the Accurium research. More than 3,000 retirement strategy scenarios were modelled across four SMSF personas, including retirees, pre-retirees, singles and couples. Researchers tested a range of portfolio allocations, retirement ages and implementation settings to determine whether incorporating lifetime income alongside a retirement bucketing strategy could improve outcomes. The results were compelling. Across every scenario tested that incorporated Allianz Retire+’s AGILE lifetime income solution, the modelling produced higher projected retirement confidence and higher projected estate values than equivalent strategies that did not. Average improvements in retirement confidence ranged from 6.7 percentage points to 13.8 percentage points, while average increases in projected estate values ranged from 33.7 per cent to 77 per cent depending on the client profile. Perhaps most surprising was that improvements in retirement confidence were accompanied by stronger estate outcomes. “Across more than 3,000 scenarios, we consistently found that incorporating AGILE within a retirement bucketing strategy improved both retirement income sustainability and projected estate outcomes,” Dunn said. “The modelling demonstrated benefits across a range of SMSF client personas, risk profiles and retirement stages, suggesting lifetime income solutions can play an important role in helping retirees manage longevity risk and sequencing risk.” One of the key drivers behind the results was a reduction in the need to sell growth assets during periods of market stress. The research found portfolios incorporating lifetime income experienced fewer instances where growth assets needed to be sold to support retirement spending. By reducing reliance on growth assets to meet ongoing income needs, more of the portfolio remained available to participate in future market recoveries. According to van der Veen, this finding is particularly relevant in the current investment environment. “Most SMSF retirees don’t suffer from a lack of investments. They suffer from a lack of income certainty,” she said. “Keeping more cash isn’t always the answer. The challenge is how to create confidence without sacrificing the growth needed to fund a retirement that could last 30 years or more.” She said elevated market uncertainty is forcing advisers to revisit some long-held retirement assumptions. “We’re seeing a world where traditional assumptions around diversification are being challenged. Equity valuations remain elevated, market shocks are arriving more frequently, and the historical relationship between equities and bonds isn’t always behaving the way advisers have come to expect.” “For retirees and those approaching retirement, sequencing risk becomes far more significant because they no longer have time on their side. The order in which returns arrive can have a profound impact on long-term retirement outcomes.” The research also identified some of the strongest benefits among couple households, which typically face longer retirement horizons and greater exposure to longevity risk. In some scenarios, projected retirement confidence increased by nearly 20 percentage points, while estate outcomes more than doubled compared with baseline strategies. Researchers also found the benefits were often more pronounced among more conservatively invested retirees, challenging the perception that lifetime income solutions are only relevant for clients with fewer assets. For advisers, the findings point towards a broader shift in retirement planning. Rather than viewing growth, income, liquidity and estate planning as competing objectives, retirement strategies may be increasingly structured around distinct purposes. In the modelling, assets were allocated across cash, income, lifetime income and growth buckets, with each component performing a specific role within the broader retirement strategy. Van der Veen said the research should not be interpreted as a challenge to traditional bucketing strategies, but rather as an evolution of them. “The findings aren’t suggesting advisers should abandon bucketing. In fact, the research demonstrated that bucketing continues to play an important role,” she said. “What we’re seeing is evidence that a source of guaranteed lifetime income can complement traditional bucketing by helping clients manage a risk that cash reserves alone can’t solve, which is the uncertainty around how long retirement will last.” As Australia’s retirement system continues to mature, advisers are increasingly being asked to deliver not just portfolios, but confidence. For SMSF members in particular, the challenge is rarely about maximising returns alone. It’s about creating a strategy capable of supporting spending goals, managing market risk and providing peace of mind over a retirement that could last decades. “Retirement planning ultimately comes back to the questions clients care most about,” Dunn said. “Can I spend confidently? Will my income last? And what happens if I live longer than expected? The research suggests that incorporating lifetime income into a retirement strategy can help advisers answer those questions more effectively.”
items.ai_summary: • **New research suggests guaranteed lifetime income is critical for retirement planning**; • **Combining bucketing with lifetime income solutions improves retirement outcomes** for SMSF members

items.title: The ‘kids’ inheriting older clients’ wealth might soon be retirees themselves
items.teaser: The conventional wisdom that the kids of advisers’ oldest clients stand to inherit their wealth might be overlooking the fact that by the time it happens these “kids” are likely to be near or in retirement themselves.
items.brief_text: For as long as most advisers can remember, one assumption has underpinned almost every business growth plan: an older client’s wealth will eventually pass to their children, and those children will need an adviser of their own. But that assumption may have a flaw, or at least a wrinkle, as revealed by Treasury’s 2026 Intergenerational Report , released on Monday. The “kids” who stand to inherit the older clients’ wealth are getting older too. Treasury’s report suggests that as clients get older, by the time their estate is actually settled their children are themselves likely to already in their late 50s or into their 60s, well established in their own careers and in fact closer to their own retirement than to buying a first home. They may be in less need of inherited wealth than their own children. So, if an advice business really wants to “freshen up” its client base by attracting younger clients just starting out on their financial journey, then maybe the onboarding efforts need to be directed at the next generation but one: the grandchildren. The Treasury report paints a clear picture of a population getting older and wealthier, and the challenges this poses both at a national level and to the financial advisers whose role is so critical to helping Australians manage both aging and getting richer. It projects Australian women will live to 89.5 years and men to 86.1 by 2065-66, with the 85-and-over cohort set to triple in size over the same period. Deaths are projected to outnumber births for the first time by the 2060s, a milestone Treasury says many advanced economies, including Japan, Germany, Italy and the Republic of Korea, have already reached. Population growth is expected to slow to 0.9 per cent a year over the next 40 years, down from 1.4 per cent over the past 40, driven mainly by a lower fertility rate. Treasury expects the economy to more than double in real terms by 2065-66. Superannuation growth Meanwhile, the report notes that superannuation assets have grown from $148 billion when the Superannuation Guarantee began in 1992 to $4.8 trillion today, and superannuation is now the second largest source of wealth for Australian households. The median superannuation balance for Australians aged 65 to 69 is projected to rise from $204,000 in 2024 to approach a nominal $450,000 by the end of the medium term. Superannuation drawdowns are projected to rise to almost 6 per cent of GDP by 2065-66. Treasury says this maturing superannuation system is reducing reliance on the Age Pension as the population ages, and that further reforms, including increases to the superannuation guarantee, paying superannuation on payday and boosting the Low Income Superannuation Tax Offset, will help take more pressure off the Age Pension in the decades ahead. Treasury also points to a government reform package covering four fronts: making the superannuation system safer, widening access to financial advice, reforming the retirement phase of superannuation, and consulting on changes to strengthen the superannuation performance test. A system asking Australians to fund a longer retirement themselves with less reliance on the state needs more people getting professional advice. That need does not stop at the client sitting across the adviser’s desk; it extends to the child managing a parent’s affairs and the grandchild about to receive money they have never had to handle before. The report also shows why aged care will increasingly become an advice staple: the number of Australians aged 65 and over will keep growing, with the fastest growth in the 85-and-over cohort, set to triple by 2065-66. Treasury says this will drive demand for care economy supports, and the Government’s response is to shift more aged care into the home setting and ask those who can afford it to contribute more towards their own care. Advisers need to plan for all of this, gain the requisite skills and advertise their expertise before it becomes a crisis, not as an afterthought or add-on when a client is suddenly facing into these issues, or is helping a parent navigate them. The key issue of housing Treasury’s figures give a sense of why the children of older clients might not need the money as urgently as the older clients’ grandchildren, and one of the key reasons is housing. “Young Australians have been locked out of the housing market as house prices have risen faster than incomes over decades,” the report says. “If home ownership rates had remained at their 1981 levels, the most recent data available indicates around 250,000 more households aged 25–34 would own their own home.” The government’s own response to these demographic and population-level challenges is a fascinating analogue to the direction advisers and advice businesses need to move. An advice practice that wants a younger client base might have been flirting with potential clients one generation too old. A client in their 80s needs advice that can see them through superannuation drawdown and aged care planning. The child in their 50s or 60s, who is still working and not yet needing the money, needs to be kept in the loop, but not necessarily chased by the practice looking for a generational refresh of its client base. The grandchild in their 20s or 30s, now locked out of home ownership and unfamiliar with managing money, might be the one who actually needs to be onboarded, and should be the focus of advisers.
items.ai_summary: • **Treasury’s 2026 Intergenerational Report** shows inheriting clients’ wealth may soon go to retirees, not younger generations. • Advisers should consider targeting grandchildren for new clients as the traditional client succession model changes.
